title: Gain-Bandwidth Trade-Offs
intro: For a one-pole amplifier, raising gain lowers bandwidth by the same factor. The product stays constant and is a better figure of merit than either alone.

blocks.text: A CS stage with a load capacitance CL has the pole 1/(RD*CL) and DC gain gm*RD. Their product is the gain-bandwidth product: GBW = gm / (2*pi*CL). Doubling RD doubles the gain but halves the bandwidth.
The only ways to raise GBW are more gm (more current or width) or less CL. This simple formula is the heart of every speed-power trade-off in analog design.

When there are several poles, adding them reduces the bandwidth beyond a single-pole estimate; the bandwidth of N identical poles is approximately sqrt(2^(1/N) - 1) times that of one. More stages mean more gain but a lower product bandwidth than the individual stages.

blocks.title: GBW
blocks.text: gm = 2 mS and CL = 200 fF. Find GBW and the -3 dB bandwidth when the gain is 20.
solution: At a gain of 20 the bandwidth is 1.59 GHz / 20 = 80 MHz.
blocks.answer: GBW = 1.6 GHz; bandwidth 80 MHz at gain 20.

blocks.title: Two identical poles
blocks.text: What is the -3 dB bandwidth of two identical cascaded one-pole stages, each with pole fp?
solution: Total |H| = 1/(1 + (f/fp)^2). The -3 dB point satisfies 1 + (f/fp)^2 = sqrt(2), so f = fp * sqrt(sqrt(2) - 1) = 0.644 fp.
